name: Determining Whether One is a Teenager (Case 2)
description: Construct a program that asks the user to enter a string that has the user name and age separated by a colon, and prints whether the user is a teenager. Make sure that the program handles all possible exceptions. The program must ask the user for an input until the user enters a string that could be processed without any exception.
code:
#Step 1: Define the function
def check_age():
    #Step 1.1: Ask for a valid input as long as the input could not be processed; otherwise stop
    processed = False
    while not processed :
        s = input("Enter the name and age, separated by a colon:")
        #Step 1.1.1: Split the given string into the name and age 
        lst = s.split(":")
        #Step 1.1.2: Enclose the code that might throw an exception within the try block
        try:
            name = lst[0]
            age = int(lst[1])
            if age >= 13 and age <= 19 :
                print(name + " is a teenager.")
            else:
                print(name + " is not a teenager.")     
            processed = True
        #Step 1.1.3: Handle all possible exceptions that may be thrown in the try block 
        except IndexError :
            print("Error! Separate the name and age by a colon.")
        except ValueError :
            print("Error! Age must be an integer.")
#Step 2: Call the function
check_age()

commentList: Purpose: This line defines a function named check_age that groups all the program steps (input loop, parsing, exception handling, and output) so you can run them together when you call the function later. It organizes the core logic and keeps the main script clean.

Syntax breakdown: def starts a function definition, check_age is the function name you choose, () are required even if the function takes no parameters, and : begins the indented block that contains the function body. Everything indented under this line belongs to the function.

Execution behaviour: When Python runs this line it creates the function object but does not execute the code inside yet. The code inside runs only when you later call check_age(), so defining the function just prepares it for use.

Common errors and misconceptions: If you omit the colon or parentheses (for example writing def check_age or def check_age:), Python raises a SyntaxError. Incorrect indentation of the following lines will raise an IndentationError. Also some learners expect the body to run immediately—remember it runs only on call.

Best practices: Give the function a clear name (check_age is fine). Add a short docstring as the first indented line to explain what the function does. For easier testing, consider making it accept input as parameters instead of always calling input() inside the function, and consider adding type hints if you want clearer interfaces.

3.content: #Step 1.1: Ask for a valid input as long as the input could not be processed; otherwise stop

commentList: You are creating a flag variable named processed and giving it the boolean value False so the program knows the input has not been successfully handled yet.
The syntax processed = False is an assignment: the name processed now refers to the boolean constant False (note the capital F).

Semantically this pairs with the next line while not processed: since processed starts as False, not processed is True and the loop will run until you set processed to True after successful processing.

A common mistake is using the string 'False' or the number 0 instead of the boolean False; while some of those may work because of truthiness, you should use the boolean constants True and False for clarity.
If you forget to initialize processed before the loop and try to test it, Python will raise an error for using an undefined variable; so you must set it before you check it.

Best practice: give the flag a clear name (e.g., input_processed or valid_input) and initialize it just before the loop. An alternative pattern is while True with a break when processing succeeds, which is also clear and idiomatic.
This line starts a loop that keeps asking the user for input until you successfully process one valid input; the loop continues as long as processed is False.

Syntax breakdown: 'while' begins the loop, 'not processed' is the loop condition that uses the boolean negation operator to check the flag, and the trailing ':' marks the start of the indented loop block that follows.

How it works in this program: because processed was set to False before the loop, the condition is True and the loop runs. Inside the try block you set processed = True when everything succeeds; at that point 'not processed' becomes False and the loop stops.

Common mistakes and pitfalls: if you forget to set processed = True when input is valid, the loop becomes an infinite loop. Another mistake is using the opposite condition (while processed) which would skip the loop, or trying to use assignment (=) in the condition (which is not allowed in Python).
Interaction with exceptions: when an exception occurs in the try block, processed remains False and the loop repeats, which is the intended behavior for re-prompting the user after an error.

Best practices: give the flag a clear name (for example done or valid_input), or use while True with a break when input is valid; strip and validate the input before splitting; and consider adding a maximum attempt count or an explicit way for the user to exit to avoid endless prompting.

6.content: s = input("Enter the name and age, separated by a colon:")
commentList: Purpose: This line asks the user to type the name and age in one line (with a colon between them) and saves whatever the user types into the variable s so the program can process it in the next steps.
Syntax and semantics: input("...") displays the prompt text and returns the entered line as a string; the = operator assigns that returned string to the variable s.
Behavior to note: input() reads the entire line up to the Enter key and does not remove extra spaces, so s may contain leading/trailing spaces or internal spaces around the colon.

Common error/misconception: input() can raise EOFError if the user sends an end-of-file (Ctrl-D/Ctrl-Z). This line is not protected by a try/except for EOFError, so the program would crash in that case unless you catch it.

Pitfall with multiple colons: if the user types more than one colon, s.split(":") (used later) will produce more than two parts. If you want only two parts (name and age), use split(':', 1) so the age part keeps any extra colons in the name portion.

Best practices: trim whitespace (e.g., s = input(...).strip() or strip the split parts later), validate the format before converting, and consider catching EOFError. Also use clear prompts and descriptive variable names like user_input for readability.

7.content: #Step 1.1.1: Split the given string into the name and age

commentList: Purpose: This line takes the raw input string s and splits it into pieces using the colon as the separator, then stores those pieces in the variable lst so you can treat the name and age separately.

Syntax and semantics: s.split(":") calls the split method on the string s and returns a list of substrings found between every ":". The = assigns that list to lst. After this line lst is a list of strings like [name_part, age_part, ...].

Potential errors and misunderstandings: If the user did not type a colon, split returns a single-item list (e.g. ['input']) and accessing lst[1] later causes an IndexError. If the input has many colons you will get more than two parts — the code still uses only lst[0] and lst[1], which may not match the user's intention.

Common misconception: split does not modify the original string s — it returns a new list. Also split(":") matches the exact colon character (it is not a regular expression). The results are strings, not numbers.

Best practices: split only once at the first colon to avoid accidental extra parts: use s.split(":", 1). Also trim whitespace from each part before using them (for example name = parts[0].strip(); age_str = parts[1].strip()) and use a clearer variable name like parts instead of lst.

Alternative validation tip: you can check len(lst) before trying to use lst[1] (for example if len(lst) < 2: print an error and continue). That gives you a clearer, earlier error message instead of relying only on the try/except later.

9.content: #Step 1.1.2: Enclose the code that might throw an exception within the try block

commentList: Purpose: You start a try block here so you can run the code that may fail (accessing lst[1] and converting it to int) and handle any errors cleanly instead of crashing the program.

Syntax and structure: 'try' is a Python keyword followed by a colon; you must put the code that can raise exceptions on the next indented lines. The corresponding except blocks (below) must be at the same indentation level as this try.

Runtime behavior: When you run the indented code under try, Python will execute it normally. If an exception occurs, execution jumps to the first matching except block. If no exception occurs, the except blocks are skipped.

Why it’s used here: You expect IndexError when lst has no second part and ValueError when int() fails, so you enclose name/age extraction and conversion in try so the program can show a helpful message and ask again.

Common mistakes to avoid: Don’t put too much unrelated code inside try — that can hide bugs. Also avoid a bare except (catching all exceptions) because it can swallow interrupts and make debugging harder.

Best practices: Keep the try block minimal (only the risky operations), use specific except clauses as done here, and consider validating input (e.g., check len(lst) and use strip()) before converting to give clearer control flow.

Control flow note: Because processed is only set to True inside the try when no exception happens, you rely on this try block to ensure the loop repeats until the input is valid. Make sure the statements that decide success remain inside the try.
You assign the first piece from the split input to the variable name so you can use the user's name later when printing (name now holds a string).
You use lst[0] because Python uses zero-based indexing: the first element of the list is at index 0; the '=' operator stores that element into the variable name.

You normally won't get an IndexError for lst[0] after s.split(':') because split always returns at least one element, but be aware that indexing a missing element would raise IndexError — this is one reason the code is inside a try/except block.
You should strip stray spaces with name = lst[0].strip() so the printed name has no leading or trailing whitespace and you avoid subtle bugs from extra spaces.
As a best practice, you can limit the split to one split with s.split(':', 1) to allow colons inside the name, and you should check that name is not empty before using it.

You assign the second part of the split input (lst[1]) converted to an integer to the variable age — this implements the core logic of turning the user-entered age text into a numeric value you can compare.
You are using list indexing (lst[1]) to get the substring after the colon, wrapping it with int(...) to convert that string into an integer, and = to store the result in age.

If the input had no colon, lst[1] would raise IndexError; if the substring is not a valid integer (for example 'fifteen' or '15.0'), int(...) raises ValueError — both are handled by the surrounding try/except in this program.

Remember that int(...) accepts surrounding whitespace (so ' 15 ' works) but does NOT parse decimals in string form ('15.0' will raise ValueError). Also int('-1') will convert but does not enforce that the age is a sensible non-negative number.

A common pitfall is splitting on every colon: if the name contains a colon or there are extra colons, split() may produce unexpected pieces. You can avoid this by using split(':', 1) or partition(':') to only split at the first colon.

Best practice: strip whitespace before conversion and validate the numeric range. For example, use age = int(lst[1].strip()) and then check age >= 0 (and optionally a max like 120) to ensure the value makes sense.

Purpose: This line checks whether the numeric age you read is in the teen range (13 through 19). If the condition is true, the program will treat the person as a teenager and run the indented block that follows.

Syntax and meaning: 'if' starts a conditional statement; 'age >= 13' tests that age is at least 13; 'and' requires both sides to be true; 'age <= 19' tests that age is at most 19; the trailing ':' begins the code block that runs when the whole condition is true.
Behavior detail: Both comparisons must be true for the if to be true, so ages 13 and 19 are included (the range is inclusive). If either comparison fails, the else block will run instead.

Common mistakes and misconceptions: Don't assume this line protects you from non-integer input — the code relies on age already being converted to an int earlier, so a failed conversion would have raised a ValueError before reaching this line. Also avoid thinking 'and' means either comparison is enough — both must hold.

Potential edge cases: Negative ages or unrealistically large ages will pass or fail solely by these numeric checks. If you want to exclude negatives, add a check like 'age >= 0' or validate the value earlier.

Best practice suggestions: In Python, you can write this more clearly as 'if 13 <= age <= 19:' which expresses the same inclusive range in a concise way. You can also use named constants (for example TEEN_MIN = 13) to avoid 'magic numbers' and make the code easier to change and read.
You use this line to tell the user that the named person is a teenager — it produces the visible program output when the age test (age >= 13 and age <= 19) is true.

You are calling the print function with an expression that concatenates the variable name and the literal string ' is a teenager.'; the + operator joins the two strings into one before print outputs it.
You should be aware that this line only runs because it is inside the if block; if the condition is false this line is skipped, so the message only appears for ages in the 13–19 range.
You might see awkward output if name is empty or has extra spaces (for example it would print ' is a teenager.'); to avoid that, strip whitespace when you assign name (e.g., name = lst[0].strip()).

You can improve clarity and safety by using string formatting instead of +, for example: print(f"{name} is a teenager."), which avoids errors if you accidentally concatenate non-strings and is easier to read.

You should note that print always adds a newline by default and that both operands must be strings for + to work; if name were not a string you'd need to convert it first (though in this code name comes from the split and will be a string).

Purpose: This else: begins the block that runs when the if condition on Line 13 (age >= 13 and age <= 19) is False — in other words, it handles the case where the user is not a teenager and the program should print that fact.

Syntax and semantics: else: must end with a colon and be indented to match its corresponding if. The statements under this else execute only when the if test fails. The print statement under it concatenates the name and the message, so it relies on name being a string and the try block having succeeded up to this point.

Common errors and misconceptions: A frequent mistake is wrong indentation so the else pairs with try/except instead of the if; that will cause a logic error or an IndentationError. Another misconception is thinking else runs when an exception occurs — it does not; if an IndexError or ValueError happens earlier, control jumps to except blocks and this else block is skipped. Also forgetting the colon after else or writing else with a condition (use elif for conditions) will cause a syntax error.

Best practices: You should keep the if/else aligned and clear. Prefer using an f-string for the message (e.g., print(f"{name} is not a teenager.")) to avoid accidental type errors when concatenating. Also strip whitespace from the split parts (name = lst[0].strip(), age = int(lst[1].strip())) so you don't get incorrect results because of extra spaces.

Behavior note: Because this else is inside the try, it only runs after successful parsing (no exceptions). If parsing fails, the except blocks handle the error and the loop asks the user again, so you only reach this else when you have a valid name and integer age.

Purpose: This line prints a clear message saying that the person (the entered name) is not a teenager when the age check in the if/else block fails. You see this output only when the age is parsed successfully and is outside the range 13–19.

What the code does (syntax): print(name + " is not a teenager.") calls Python's print function and uses the + operator to join the value of name and the literal string " is not a teenager." into one string to display.
Why the leading space matters: the literal starts with a space (" is not ...") so the name and the message are separated correctly. If you remove that space the name and the text would run together.

When this line runs: it executes inside the try block right after you successfully set name and age and the condition (age >= 13 and age <= 19) evaluated to False. If parsing failed earlier, one of the except blocks would run instead.

Possible errors and misconceptions: concatenation (using +) requires both operands to be strings. If name were not a string you would get a TypeError. In this program name is taken from split() so it will normally be a string, but if you later change how name is obtained you must be careful.

Best practices you should follow: prefer clearer formatting such as an f-string print(f"{name} is not a teenager.") or print(name, "is not a teenager.") which automatically adds a space and converts non-strings. Also consider doing name = name.strip() earlier to remove extra spaces and check that name is not empty before printing.
Small detail to watch: the message ends with a period — keep messages consistent across branches (the 'is a teenager' branch has the same punctuation) to make program output predictable.
This line marks that the input has been handled successfully: by setting processed to True you cause the while not processed loop to stop prompting the user.

In terms of syntax and semantics, this is a simple assignment that changes the boolean variable processed from False to True; the while loop checks this variable each iteration, so changing it controls the loop flow.

Watch out for indentation and placement: because this line is inside the try block it only runs when no exception was raised. If you accidentally place it outside the try (or forget it), you may stop the loop too early or create an infinite loop respectively.

Common misconception: this line does not validate input by itself — it only signals success after your checks and conversions (like int(lst[1])) have completed without error. If you set it before validation, you can accept bad input.

Best practices: keep this assignment exactly where you know processing is complete, or alternatively use return (to exit the function) or break (to exit the loop) for clearer control flow. Also use a clear flag name (e.g., valid_input) and ensure correct indentation so you don’t change behavior by mistake.

18.content: #Step 1.1.3: Handle all possible exceptions that may be thrown in the try block

commentList: Purpose: This line starts a handler that catches an IndexError so your program does not crash when the code in the try block tries to access lst[1] but that element does not exist (for example, the user did not enter a colon or forgot the age).
Syntax: 'except IndexError :' labels a block that runs only if an IndexError was raised in the matching try block; the colon marks the start of the handler and the handler must be indented under it.
Behavior: If an IndexError occurs, execution jumps here, the print below runs, and because processed is not set to True the outer while loop continues and you are asked for input again.

Common misconceptions / pitfalls: Don't assume this catches other problems like non-integer ages — those raise ValueError and are handled by a different except. Also avoid using a bare except (which catches everything); being specific like IndexError helps you diagnose input problems.

Best practices: Instead of relying only on catching IndexError, you can proactively check the split result (e.g., if len(lst) < 2) before indexing, or use s.split(':', 1) and .strip() to handle extra colons and spaces. Keep the error message clear so the user knows how to fix their input.

20.content: print("Error! Separate the name and age by a colon.")
commentList: This line shows a user-facing error when the program catches an IndexError: it tells you that the input did not contain both name and age separated by a colon, so you need to enter them in the form name:age.

Technically, print(...) is inside the except IndexError block. When the code tries to do lst[1] but the split produced too few parts, Python raises IndexError and control jumps here; print outputs the message and then the while loop repeats because processed is still False.

A common misconception is thinking this message also handles non-integer ages — it does not. This except only handles missing parts (no colon or missing age). A ValueError (non-integer age) is handled by a different except on line 21.

Another subtle case: if the user types extra colons, lst[1] may still exist so this message won't run even if the input is malformed in another way. To allow colons in names, you might use split(':', 1) instead so the right side is treated as the age.

Best practices: make the message clear and friendly (as it is), but also consider validating the split length before indexing (so you don't rely only on exceptions), strip whitespace from parts, and prompt examples in the input request to reduce repeated errors.
This line starts an exception handler that catches ValueError exceptions so the program does not crash when int(lst[1]) fails; it lets you handle the bad input and keep asking the user.
Syntax breakdown: 'except ValueError :' means 'if a ValueError is raised in the try block, run the indented code that follows'; the colon begins the handler block just like for if/while/def.

How it helps the solution: when the age part cannot be converted to an integer (for example 'twelve' or '12.5'), this handler runs and allows the loop to continue prompting you until a correct input is given.

Common misconceptions and pitfalls: this only catches ValueError — it will not catch an IndexError (missing colon) or other errors. Also note that int(' 12 ') is fine, but int('12.0') and int('twelve') cause ValueError.

Best practices for you: be specific with exceptions (as done here) instead of using a bare except. Consider using 'except ValueError as e:' if you want to inspect the error, or validate/strip the age string before conversion (e.g., age_str = lst[1].strip()) to give clearer feedback.

22.content: print("Error! Age must be an integer.")
commentList: This line runs when Python raises a ValueError during the try block; it tells you that the conversion to integer failed and that the age you entered was not an integer.

Syntactically, this is a print statement inside the except ValueError block—so it only executes if int(lst[1]) raised ValueError. It does not change processed, so the while loop will ask you for input again.

Common misconception: ValueError can occur for more than just alphabetic text — it also happens for an empty string, a float like '18.0', or other non-integer formats. It is not raised when the colon is missing (that gives IndexError instead).
Be careful not to use a bare except (except:), because that would hide other bugs. This specific except only catches conversion problems, which is what you want here.

Best practice: make the error message helpful. You could strip whitespace before converting, show the invalid value in the message, or validate with methods like str.isdigit() before int() to give clearer guidance to the user.
Also consider logging the original input for debugging and keep the program asking for input (as this line does) until a valid integer age is provided.

You must not forget the parentheses: writing check_age without () only gives you the function object instead of running it. Also, if the function definition appeared after this line you would get a NameError, so ensure the function is defined first.

You should be aware that calling check_age() runs input(), so in non-interactive environments input() may block or raise EOFError. To avoid automatic execution when someone imports this file, put the call under if __name__ == '__main__':

You can rely on the function's internal try/except to handle IndexError and ValueError, but calling it here can still lead to an infinite prompt if the user never provides valid input. As a best practice, consider adding a quit option, a retry limit, or catching EOFError to stop gracefully.
